\chapter{Short Replies}
\label{ch:hi-replies}
\hlchaptermodality{48}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer someone in Hindi with one word, and pick how certain that one word sounds.}

Complete HI-C48-absolutely and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sac]{\hi{सच} (sac) — true}

\label{lesson:HI-C48-true}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{mehmān} mean, and what did \emph{paṛosī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सच}}
\textbf{\hi{सच}} (\emph{sac}) — \textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{satya}, 'true, real', worn down to a single syllable — and \emph{satya} is itself built on \emph{sat}, the participle of the verb 'to be'. What is true, at the bottom of this word, is simply what is.

Hindi keeps the long form as well, in names and in solemn speech, so one idea can arrive dressed either way. \hi{सच} is the one you say when somebody tells you something you did not expect.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five short replies.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sac}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sac}, then \emph{paṛosī}, so the reply and the person sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{सच} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}true\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bas]{\hi{बस} (bas) — enough, that's all}

\label{lesson:HI-C48-enough}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sac} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बस}}
\textbf{\hi{बस}} (\emph{bas}) — \textquotedblleft{}enough, that's all\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{bas}, 'enough'. One syllable that stops a pouring hand, ends a list, or closes an argument, and it does all three on tone alone.

Doubled, \emph{bas bas}, it is the polite way to say enough while somebody is still serving you. Stretched out, it is what you say when they are plainly not listening. Very few words in the language do this much work for so little.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and both are one syllable.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bas}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bas}, then \emph{sac}, one after the other, as answers
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बस} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}enough, that's all\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zarūr]{\hi{ज़रूर} (zarūr) — certainly}

\label{lesson:HI-C48-certainly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bas} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{ज़रूर}}
\textbf{\hi{ज़रूर}} (\emph{zarūr}) — \textquotedblleft{}certainly\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{ḍarūr}, 'necessity', arriving through Persian — and the word has walked from necessity to certainty by the shortest possible route: what must be, will be. Its relative \emph{zarūrat} is still the plain Hindi word for a need.

The dot written under the \hi{ज़} marks a sound that came in with the Persian layer rather than down from Sanskrit. The letter underneath it was already here; the dot is the passport.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: true, enough, certainly.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{zarūr}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{zarūr}, then \emph{bas}, then \emph{sac}, back down the run
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{ज़रूर} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}certainly\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śāyad]{\hi{शायद} (śāyad) — perhaps}

\label{lesson:HI-C48-perhaps}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{zarūr} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{शायद}}
\textbf{\hi{शायद}} (\emph{śāyad}) — \textquotedblleft{}perhaps\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{shāyad}, 'it may be', out of \emph{shāyistan}, 'to be fitting, to be possible'. A whole conjugated form collapsed into a single hedge.

The inherited alternative is \emph{sambhavataḥ}, four syllables of Sanskrit that belong to written prose and to careful speeches. When somebody is guessing out loud in a kitchen, they say \hi{शायद}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one takes a step back.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śāyad}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{śāyad}, then \emph{zarūr}, the two ends of how sure you are
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{शायद} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}perhaps\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bilkul]{\hi{बिलकुल} (bilkul) — absolutely}

\label{lesson:HI-C48-absolutely}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{śāyad} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बिलकुल}}
\textbf{\hi{बिलकुल}} (\emph{bilkul}) — \textquotedblleft{}absolutely\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{bi-l-kull}, 'with the whole' — a preposition, the definite article \emph{al-}, and \emph{kull}, 'all', fused into one Hindi word. That same \emph{al-} is sitting, equally hidden, inside \hi{अलविदा}.

It answers a yes-or-no question with more weight than a bare yes. Put \emph{nahīṁ} after it and it does exactly the same for no, which makes it the most emphatic thing on this page in either direction.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: true, enough, certainly, perhaps, absolutely.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bilkul}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{sac}, \emph{bas}, \emph{zarūr}, \emph{śāyad}, \emph{bilkul}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बिलकुल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}absolutely\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
